prompt: In leader-follower replication, what do followers scale?

options.text: Writes
Reads
Both equally
Neither

explanation: Every write still goes through the leader and every follower applies it.

prompt: What's the main risk of asynchronous replication?

options.text: Every write is slowed down because it must wait for all followers
Acknowledged writes not yet copied are lost if the leader dies
Followers can't serve any reads until they're fully caught up
It only works when replicas sit in at least three data centres

explanation: Async replication acknowledges the client before followers have the data, so a leader crash can lose acknowledged writes. Waiting for all followers is synchronous replication, lagging followers still serve (possibly stale) reads, and there's no data-centre requirement.

prompt: A leader takes 5,000 writes/s and async followers lag 200 ms. Roughly how many acknowledged writes could failover lose?

options.text: None

prompt: What does semi-synchronous replication wait for?

options.text: Every follower to acknowledge before the write is confirmed
At least one follower to acknowledge before confirming
No followers at all; it confirms as soon as the leader writes
A full backup snapshot to finish before the commit returns

explanation: Semi-sync waits for one follower's ack, which bounds data loss without waiting for every follower. Waiting for all is fully synchronous, waiting for none is async, and backups are unrelated to commit acknowledgement.

prompt: Which guarantee is missing and what's a fix?
scenario: A user changes their display name. The page reloads, reads from a follower, and shows the old name. Refreshing a few seconds later shows the new one.

options.text: Atomicity; wrap the rename and the page read in one transaction
Read-your-writes; read the user's own data from the leader
Durability; add disks so the follower stores the write sooner
Monotonic reads; add more followers so lag drops for everyone

explanation: The user's own write hasn't reached the follower yet: a read-your-writes gap. Route their own reads to the leader (or wait for their last write position). Atomicity and durability aren't broken (the write committed), and monotonic reads is about going backwards between reads; more followers don't remove lag.

prompt: Which guarantee is broken and what fixes it?
scenario: A user refreshes a thread twice. The first load shows 12 comments; the second shows 10. Reads are load-balanced randomly across 4 followers.

options.text: Read-your-writes; send every read to the leader
Monotonic reads; pin each user to one follower
Split brain; add fencing for the old leader
Durability; switch to synchronous replication

explanation: Different followers at different lag make time go backwards between reads: a monotonic-reads violation. Pinning each user to one follower fixes it. The user didn't write anything (not read-your-writes), there's only one leader (no split brain), and no data was lost.

prompt: What has happened and what prevents it?
scenario: A network partition separates the leader from its two followers. The followers promote one of themselves. The old leader keeps accepting writes from app servers on its side. When the network heals, both have different new orders.

options.text: Replication lag; add more followers so each one catches up faster
Split brain; use quorum-based election and fence the old leader
A distributed deadlock; abort one side's writes and retry them later
Normal failover; the orders simply merge once the network heals

explanation: Two leaders accepted writes at once: split brain. Requiring a majority to elect a leader, and fencing a cut-off leader so it can't act, prevents it. It isn't lag or a deadlock, and divergent writes don't merge on their own.

prompt: Why not set the failure-detection timeout to 1 second?

options.text: One second is too slow; failover should start within milliseconds
Brief hiccups would trigger needless failovers, each risking data loss
Most databases forbid detection timeouts shorter than ten seconds
Heartbeats are only sent once a minute, so 1 s would always fire

explanation: Too short a timeout turns GC pauses and network blips into failovers, and each one risks losing unreplicated writes and disrupting clients (flapping). One second is aggressive, not slow, and there is no universal minimum or fixed one-minute heartbeat.

prompt: What's the main problem multi-leader replication introduces?

options.text: Writes become slower in every region since all leaders must agree
Concurrent writes to the same record in different leaders conflict
Reads stop working in a region whenever another leader is offline
It requires synchronous links between regions to stay consistent

explanation: Each leader accepts writes independently, so concurrent edits to the same record conflict and need resolution (last-write-wins, merging or app logic). Leaders don't wait for each other, regions keep serving when one is down, and replication between them is usually async.

prompt: With N = 3, which W and R guarantee reads overlap the latest acknowledged write?
explanation: W + R = 4 > 3. The others don't satisfy W + R > N.

prompt: How do leaderless systems repair stale replicas? Select all that apply.

options.text: Read repair during client reads
Anti-entropy background syncing
Failover to a promoted replica
Leader-driven log replay to followers

explanation: Read repair (fixing stale replicas spotted during a read) and anti-entropy (background comparison, e.g. Merkle trees) both bring replicas back in sync. Leaderless systems have no leader to fail over to or to replay a log from.
